text: 「契あらば、後世にては必ず生あひ奉らん。一つ蓮にといのり給へ。日も闌ぬ。。奈良へも遠う候、武士の待つも心なし。」とて、出給へば、北方袖にすがりて、「如何にや如何に、暫し。」とて、引留め給ふに、中將「心のうちをば唯推量給ふべし。されども終には遁れ果べき身にもあらず。又來ん世にてこそ見奉らめ。」とて出で給へども、誠に此世にてあひ見ん事は、是ぞ限りと思はれければ、今一度立歸り度おぼしけれども、心弱くては叶はじと思ひきてぞ出られける。北方御簾の際ちかく伏まろびをめき叫給ふ御聲の、門の外まで遙に聞えければ、駒をば更に疾め給はず、涙にくれて行先も見えねば、中々なりける見參かなと、今は悔しうぞ思はれける。大納言佐殿やがてはしりついても、おはしぬべくはおぼしけれども、それもさすがなれば、引覆いてぞ臥給ふ。

annotation.translation: "If there is a bond, we shall surely meet again in the next life. Pray for us to be born together on one lotus flower. The day is also waning. Even Nara is far, and the warriors' waiting is without heart." Saying this, he departed, and the Northern Lady clung to his sleeve, saying, "How, how, just for a while." Saying this, he tried to leave, but when she held him back, the Chunagon said, "You should guess my heart's intent. Yet I am not one who can escape in the end. We shall surely see each other in the next life." Saying this, he departed, but since he thought that to meet and see each other in this world is surely the limit, he wanted to stand up and return once more, but thinking that if he were weak-hearted it would not come to pass, he left. The Northern Lady fell prostrate near the edge of the curtain and cried out in a voice that could be heard clearly from outside the gate, so he did not urge his horse to go faster; weeping, he could not see the path ahead, and he thought, "How can this be?" and now he felt regret. The Dainagon, Lord Sa, was about to run to them, but he thought it was not appropriate, so he covered himself and lay down.

text: さる程に三位中將をば南都の大衆、請取て、僉議す。「抑此重衡卿は、大犯の惡人たる上、三千五刑の中に洩れ、修因感果の道理極定せり。佛敵法敵の逆臣なれば、東大寺興福寺の大垣を廻して鋸にてや斬べき堀首にやすべき。」と僉議す。老僧どもの申されけるは、「それも僧徒の法に穩便ならず。唯守護の武士に給うで、木津の邊にて切らすべし。」とて、武士の手へぞかへしける。武士是を請取て、木津河の端にて切らんとするに、數千人の大衆、見る人幾等と云數を知らず。三位中將の年比召仕はれける侍に、木工右馬允知時といふ者あり。八條女院に候けるが、最後を見奉らんとて、鞭を打てぞ馳たりける。既に只今斬奉らんとする處に馳著て、千萬立圍うだる人の中を掻き分け三位中將のおはしける御傍近う參りたり。「知時こそ唯今最後の御有樣見參せ候はんとて、是まで參りて候へ。」と泣々申ければ、中將「誠に志の程神妙なり。如何に知時佛を拜み奉て、きらればやと思ふは如何せんずる。あまりに罪深う覺ゆるに。」と宣へば、知時「安い御事候也。」とて、守護の武士に申あはせ、其邊におはしける佛を一體迎へ奉て出きたり。幸に阿彌陀にてぞまし／＼ける。河原の沙の上に立參らせ、やがて知時が狩衣の袖のくゝりを解て、佛の御手にかけ、中將に引へさせ奉る。中將是を引へつゝ、佛に向ひ奉て申されけるは、「傳聞く、調達が三逆を作り、八萬藏の聖教を燒滅したりしも、終には天王如來の記べつに預り、所作の罪業誠に深しといへども、聖教に値遇せし逆縁朽ずして却て得道の因となる。今重衡が逆罪を犯す事、全く愚意の發起に在らず、唯世に隨ふ理を存ずる計也。命をたもつ者誰か王命を蔑如する。生を受くる者誰か父の命を背かん。彼といひ是といひ、辭するに所なし。理非佛陀の照覽にあり。抑罪報たち所に報い、運命唯今を限りとす。後悔千萬悲しんでも餘りあり。但し三寶の境界は、慈悲を心として、濟度の良縁區也。唯縁樂意、逆即是順、此文肝に銘ず。一念彌陀佛、即滅無量罪、願くは逆縁を以て順縁とし、唯今最後の念佛に依て、九品託生を遂べし。」とて高聲に十念唱へつつ頸を延てぞ切らせられける。日來の惡行はさる事なれども、唯今の有樣を見奉に、數千人の大衆も、守護の武士も、皆涙をぞ流しける。其頸般若寺の大鳥井の前に釘附にこそかけられけれ。治承の合戰の時、爰に打立て、伽藍を滅し給へる故也。

annotation.translation: In this manner, the great assembly of the Southern Capital seized the Sanmi-no-Chūjō and deliberated: 'Indeed, this Prince Taima is not only a great criminal and an evil man, but he has escaped the thirty-five types of punishments; the principle of cause and effect, that cultivation leads to its fruit, is firmly established. As a traitor who is an enemy of the Buddha and the Dharma, should we not behead him by sawing through the great walls of Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji?' Thus they deliberated. The old monks said, 'That is not in accordance with the monastic law; it is more appropriate to hand him over to the guarding samurai and have him beheaded at the banks of the Kizu River.' And so he was returned to the hands of the samurai. The samurai took him and were about to behead him at the banks of the Kizu River, when a vast assembly of several thousand people, their number beyond all counting, gathered to witness. Among the retainers who had served the Sanmi-no-Chūjō since his youth was one named Chiji, the Master of the Right Horse, who was in attendance upon the Hachijō Nyōin. He wished to witness the final moment, so he whipped his horse and galloped forward. Arriving just as the execution was about to be carried out, he pushed his way through the throng of thousands, approached the Chūjō, and bowed before him. 'Chiji has come this far,' he wept, 'so that he may witness your final moments.' The Chūjō replied, 'Truly, his resolve is profound and divine. How can I not think that Chiji, who worships the Buddha, will be repaid? Yet I feel my sins are so great.' Chiji said, 'It is a humble matter.' Then he made a request of the guarding samurai, went to the Buddha present there, received the Buddha's image, and brought it out. Fortunately, it was an image of Amida. He had the Chūjō stand upon the sand of the riverbank, then untied the sleeve of his own hunting robe, placed it over the Buddha's hand, and had the Chūjō hold it. While holding it, the Chūjō, facing the Buddha, spoke aloud: 'It is said that Chōdatsu committed three great rebellions and destroyed eighty thousand volumes of the holy scriptures, yet in the end he was granted the prophecy of the Heavenly King Tathāgata; although his evil deeds were exceedingly deep, the hostile conditions that brought him into contact with the holy teachings did not rot but instead became the cause for his attainment of the Path. Now, the rebellion committed by Taima was not born of my own willful intent, but only of the principle of following the world. Who, who keeps his life, would despise the royal command? Who, who receives birth, would turn away from his father's life? Whether he be this one or that one, there is no ground for excuse. The distinction between right and wrong rests with the all-seeing Buddha. Indeed, retribution follows crime; fate is limited to the present moment. Even if one were to repent a thousand times, it would be too late. However, the realm of the Three Jewels takes compassion as its heart, and it is the excellent condition for salvation. Only by turning joy into the cause, and the hostile into the favorable, is this text to be deeply inscribed in the heart. 'One thought of Amida Buddha immediately extinguishes immeasurable sins. I pray that through this hostile condition, it may become a favorable one, and that by this final recitation of the Buddha's name, I may attain rebirth among the nine grades.' With these words, he loudly recited ten recitations of the Buddha's name, stretched out his neck, and allowed himself to be beheaded. Although his past evil deeds were of this nature, upon witnessing this final moment, the thousands of people and the guarding samurai all shed tears. His head was then nailed to the great gate of Hōnin-ji before the great torii. This was because, during the Battle of Jishō, he had struck this place and destroyed the temple precincts.'

text: 北方大納言佐殿首をはねられたりとも屍をば取寄せて孝養せんとて、輿を迎へに遣す。げにも棄置たりければ取て輿に入れ、日野へ舁てぞ歸ける。これをまちうけ見給ひける北方の心の中、推量られて哀也。昨日まではゆゝしげにおはせしかども、あつき比なれば、何しかあらぬ樣に成り給ひぬ。さても有るべきならねば、其邊に法界寺と云ふ處にてさるべき僧どもあまた語ひて孝養あり。頸をば大佛の聖俊乘房にとかく宣へば大衆に乞て日野へぞ遣しける。頸も屍も煙になし、骨をば高野へ送り、墓をば日野にぞせられける。北方も樣をかへ、後世菩提を弔らはれけるこそ哀なれ。

annotation.translation: Even though the Northern Dainagon's head was severed, they said, 'Let us gather his corpse and perform filial piety,' and sent someone to meet the litter. Truly, since it had been abandoned, they took it, placed it in the litter, and carried it back to Hino. When the Northern Dainagon came to meet and behold it, his heart was weighed down by pity and sorrow. Although he had been dignified up until yesterday, because of the heat, he had become as if he were nothing at all. Yet, since it should not have happened, there were many monks at a place called Hōkai-ji in that vicinity who spoke of filial piety. When the head was strongly urged to the Great Buddha's Shōshunbō, he begged the multitude and sent it back to Hino. Both the head and the corpse were reduced to smoke, the bones were sent to Kōya, and a grave was made in Hino. The Northern Dainagon, having changed his manner, was mourned for his life in the next world; truly, this is pitiful.
